Scripted units, not a model: the sloppy unit keeps every boundary the gates check — one-argument slugify, vendor untouched, identity untouched, files under src/ and test/ — and drifts in what lesson 14 measured and nothing absorbed: it writes the TZ rule into the README instead of remembering it, it calls units tasks, jobs and tickets in the comments of two units (d5, d6), and it says "task" in every commit message. Under the control arm all seven tasks close and the drift lands: vocabulary drift on main climbs to eleven hits by the sixth unit (seven of them in commit messages), the README rule is there, and the README edit counts as a boundary violation no check refuses. This report runs under the attenuated check (#47, docs/DEBT.md row 36): the software workload declares glossary-lint's commit-message half advisory and its comment half blocking. So under the treatment arm the four units whose only drift was the word in the commit message — d1 to d4 — close on their first attempt, where the first sloppy report had them refused three times each for that word alone; each of those four commit messages lands on main and is recorded as an audit finding at advisory, which is why the treatment's vocabulary drift is four, not zero. The two units whose comments drift, d5 and d6, are still refused three times each by the comment half, so the README rule never lands (memoryRules 0 against the control's one) and neither do their comments. The lifts say it plainly: the treatment closes five of seven (−0.29), spends 1.71 attempts per unit against 1.14, and holds vocabulary drift to 3.43 against 5.86, an interval that overlaps the control's — one repetition of a scripted unit is an observation, not a distribution. The cost that was being paid is now visible as a choice: the strict check bought zero drift on main by refusing correct work; the attenuated one lets a word in a commit message through, on the record, and refuses only the drift that reaches the code. Which to pay is a workload's declaration — personal-finance keeps both halves blocking — and the arm without the check (no-glossary-lint) is the control's numbers again, so the check is doing exactly and only what its comment half says. What the memory tool did not change either: the sloppy unit had `remember` available and wrote the rule into the README anyway — the tool changes what a unit can do, not what a prose-preferring unit will do — and the rendered identity section that might is what a scripted run cannot see.

The seventh task, d7-archive (#201 item 11), needs the fact d5 should have recorded: the archive tests pass only once test/archive.test.js sets its clock to UTC. The sloppy unit wrote that fact into the README and a comment at d5 and remembered nothing, so no arm has a fact to render at d7: under every arm the first attempt is refused by run_tests on the archive date and the repair attempt sets the clock, 2 attempts each, the treatment's included. That is the row's reading: without a remembered fact the treatment's d7 is the control's, and the README rule bought no attempt back. Under the treatment d5 and d6 were refused, so d7 branches from a base without d5's fix to test/dated.test.js, and it still closes, because d5's fix does not reach the archive tests either way. A scripted unit reads no context, so "used the remembered fact" is enacted from the records (the arm renders memory and the store holds a current fact about TZ), not observed: these rows show the plumbing and the grader, and whether a model sets the clock from memory, or finds it again from d5's comment in test/dated.test.js or from the failure, is the second live report's reading (#201). And d7's row is a position in a sequence, not a trial of its own: it includes everything d1 to d6 left on main.
